title: Mourning Together
hook: Men often grieve best side by side, in rituals, tasks and shared silence, and the friend who simply turns up is remembered for decades.
why:
When a man's father, child, partner or friend dies, the men around him often do not know what to do. They worry about saying the wrong thing, so they say nothing. They worry about intruding, so they stay away. They send a message, attend the funeral, and then, after a few weeks, the calls stop. Years later, bereaved men often say that they remember exactly who turned up, and who did not.

The chapter on grief in Part II described what grief does to a body and how people grieve in different styles. This chapter is about mourning: the shared, visible, physical things people do together after a death. It covers why mourning together suits many men; what research says about rituals; how to turn up and what to do when you get there; the old wisdom of waiting for the mourner to speak; keeping the dead person's name alive; staying for the months after the funeral; and how, at a graveside, everything this part has taught comes together.

teach.p:
The chapter on grief in Part II described Terry Martin and Kenneth Doka's distinction between intuitive grief, expressed through feeling and talk, and instrumental grief, expressed through thinking and doing. Many men lean toward the instrumental: they grieve by building the coffin, organising the funeral, fixing the widow's boiler, writing the eulogy. That is not a failure to grieve. It is a way of grieving, and it is often done best alongside other people.

Mourning gives men forms for grief that do not depend on words. Carrying a coffin on your shoulder with five other men. Throwing a handful of earth. Standing in a row with your head bowed. Raising a glass. Shaking every hand at the door of the church. These are ways of saying something that most men could not say aloud, and of saying it together.

The opening chapter of this part described the side-by-side principle. Mourning is perhaps its purest form: men standing shoulder to shoulder, looking at the same thing, carrying the same weight, often in silence. The chapter on personal space described how shared identity shrinks the gap between men; grief does the same. Men who would never touch each other otherwise put their arms around one another at a graveside.

The figures here stand in a row, heads bowed, one with an arm across the shoulders of the man beside him. Nothing is being said. A great deal is being shared.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men grieved as well alone as together. Research on grieving styles suggests that many men prefer action and shared tasks to talk, but the benefits of mourning together specifically have not been measured directly, so treat this as a well-grounded claim rather than a finding.

teach.h: Rituals give the body something to do.
teach.p:
In 2014 Michael Norton and Francesca Gino asked people who had lost a loved one, a relationship or, in a laboratory version, a lottery prize, about the rituals they had performed afterwards. People who had performed a ritual reported less grief, and the effect held even among people who said they did not believe that rituals worked. Most of the rituals people described were private and personal: visiting a place, playing a song, lighting a candle. Norton and Gino suggested that rituals help by restoring a sense of control after a loss that leaves people feeling powerless.

The wider evidence is more mixed. A review of studies before the pandemic found little consistent link between taking part in grief rituals and how grief unfolded over time. During the pandemic, when funerals were restricted, Lonneke Mitima-Verloop and her colleagues found that whether people attended a funeral, and how they felt about it, was related to their later grief symptoms, while other rituals were not. Many found alternative rituals helpful in their own way.

So rituals are not a cure, and their effects vary. But they give the body something to do at a time when nothing can be done, and many people find that they help. Funerals, wakes, graveside visits, anniversaries, a pint poured for someone who is not there: these are forms men can use without having to invent them.

The figure here bows his head. Ritual turns that movement from a private collapse into a shared act.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if rituals made no difference to how people felt after a loss. Norton and Gino found that they reduced grief, but wider evidence on rituals and longer-term grief is mixed, so their benefit is real for many but not guaranteed.

teach.p:
The single most important thing you can do when someone you know is bereaved is to turn up. Go to the funeral. Go to the house. Bereaved people often say afterwards that they cannot remember what anyone said, but they remember exactly who was there.

When you arrive, greet the bereaved person in the way the chapters on greetings and hugs described, matching what they offer and leaning toward warmth: a handshake held a moment longer, a hand on the arm, a hug if they open their arms. Say one short, true sentence: “I'm so sorry.” “He was a good man.” “I'm here.” You do not need anything cleverer, and you should avoid anything that explains or minimises the loss: “He's in a better place,” “At least he didn't suffer,” “Everything happens for a reason.”

Then stay nearby. Stand with them, or near them, at the edge of things. Watch for something practical to do: a coat to hold, a car to fetch, a drink to pour, a relative who needs a lift. The chapter on shared activity described how men often show care through doing, and grief is a time when doing is welcome. In the days after, the casserole, the mown lawn and the school run are forms of mourning too.

The figures here stand side by side, one with a hand resting on the other's shoulder while he bows his head. That is often all turning up looks like, and it is enough.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if bereaved people valued attendance less than the right words. Accounts from the bereaved consistently emphasise presence over language, though this rests on testimony and experience rather than controlled research.
teach.pullQuote: Bereaved people rarely remember what anyone said. They remember exactly who was there.

teach.p:
Jewish tradition has a custom for visitors to a house of mourning during shiva, the first week after a burial. Visitors traditionally come in, sit, and wait for the mourner to speak first. The custom is traced to the friends of Job in the Bible, who sat with him in silence for seven days before anyone spoke. The reasoning is practical: a visitor cannot know what the mourner needs at that moment, whether to talk about the dead person, to talk about something else, or to sit in silence, and waiting lets the mourner decide.

Many traditions share the instinct. The chapter on silence described Keith Basso's account of Western Apache people falling silent in the presence of grief. The principle travels well beyond its origins: come, sit, and let them set the agenda.

In practice, this means arriving without a speech prepared. Sit down near the bereaved man, at his level. Let a silence be a silence. If he talks about the dead person, listen, nod, ask a gentle question. If he talks about the football, talk about the football. If he says nothing, say nothing with him for a while. When he signals that he is tired, by a look, a nod or standing up, go, and say that you will come back.

The figures here sit side by side on a bench. One of the most useful things a man can do for a grieving friend is to sit like this and wait for him to decide what happens next.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if bereaved people generally preferred visitors to lead the conversation. The custom rests on long tradition and on the experience of mourners rather than research, and some bereaved people do want visitors to take the lead, so read the person in front of you.

teach.p:
Many men avoid saying a dead person's name to the bereaved, afraid that it will open a wound. Most bereaved people say the opposite: what hurts is the silence, the sense that the person they loved has been erased from everyone else's conversation.

In 1996 Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman published a collection of studies challenging the older view that healthy grief means letting go of the dead. They argued that many bereaved people keep a continuing bond with the person who has died, through memories, conversations, rituals and a sense of their presence, and that this bond is often a resource rather than a sign of being stuck.

So say the name. Tell a story about them. Laugh about the time they did something ridiculous. Ask the bereaved man about them: what they were like as a boy, what they would have said about the match. Mark the dates that matter: the birthday, the anniversary of the death, the first Christmas. A short message on those days, “Thinking of you and of Jamie today,” is remembered for years.

The figure here stands with his head down, alone with a memory. A friend who comes and says the name out loud brings that memory back into the shared world, where it can be carried by more than one person.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if bereaved people generally preferred the dead not to be mentioned. Research on continuing bonds and accounts of the bereaved suggest the opposite, though some people at some moments need a break from talking about their loss.

teach.p:
In the first week after a death, there are visitors, flowers and food. By the third month, most of it has gone, and the world expects the bereaved person to be getting back to normal. For many people, this is when the hardest part begins. The numbness wears off, and the full weight of the loss arrives just as everyone else has moved on.

So keep turning up. Keep inviting him to the things you used to do together, even when he says no, as the chapter on shared activity suggested. A walk, a match, a pint, a job that needs doing: side by side, at his pace, with room for the subject to come up or not. The chapter on grief described the waves of grief that arrive without warning, often triggered by an anniversary, a song or a smell; a friend who knows about them can be ready.

Watch, too, for grief that is turning into something else, using what Part II taught: drinking that is creeping up, a man who has stopped looking after himself, withdrawal that is deepening rather than easing. If you are worried that a grieving friend is thinking about suicide, ask him directly, as the chapter on suicidal thoughts described, and use the crisis resources in this app. Men bereaved by suicide carry a particularly heavy grief, and support groups exist specifically for them.

The figures here walk side by side, months after the funeral. The friend who is still walking beside a bereaved man in the spring is the one he will remember.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if bereaved people needed less support as the months passed. Accounts of bereavement and research on grief's course suggest that many need sustained support, though grief varies widely and many people recover well with ordinary help.

teach.p:
This part of the book began with two men side by side in a car and ends with men side by side at a grave. Between the two, it has described a language men use with each other without ever being taught it: the side-by-side conversation, the greeting, the nod, the space kept and closed, the hug and its slaps, touch in disguise and touch offered plainly, silence that comforts, the shared task, the hard limits of attraction and consent, disagreement and repair, holding a child, sitting with the sick.

At a funeral, all of it is used at once. A man greets a widow and matches her offer. He nods to an old friend across the church. He stands closer to other men than he would anywhere else. He hugs, and when the other man holds on, he stops slapping and stays still. He touches a shoulder and lets the hand rest. He sits in silence and lets the mourner speak first. He carries, digs, pours, drives. He says the name. He comes back.

None of this requires eloquence. It requires a body that knows how to be present, and a willingness to use it on the worst day of another man's life. That is the point of everything in this part: not reading other men for advantage, but knowing how to stand beside them.

The figures here stand together from behind, one with an arm across the other's shoulders while he bows his head. If a man learns only one thing from this part of the book, it might be how to stand like this, and when.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the skills in this part made no difference to how well men could support each other in grief. That is a claim about practice rather than a measured result, and its test is whether the men you stand beside find you useful.

caseStudy:
Chris, fifty, has three friends from school: Ade, Simon and Mike. They play golf badly twice a year and share a group chat that is mostly about football. In June, Chris's son Jamie, nineteen, is killed in a car crash.

Ade drives straight round and sits in the kitchen for three hours, mostly in silence, making tea. Simon handles the phone calls Chris cannot face. Mike, who has never known what to say to anyone in pain, sends a message and then stays away, telling himself the family needs space.

At the funeral, Chris asks the three of them to help carry the coffin. Mike almost says no, then does it. Under the weight, shoulder to shoulder with the others, walking in step, he feels something give way. At the graveside he stands beside Chris with his arm across his shoulders, and neither of them says a word.

In the months after, the visits thin out. Ade keeps texting invitations to the golf; Chris keeps saying no, and Ade keeps asking. Mike sets a reminder in his phone for Jamie's birthday in October. On the day he sends a message: “Thinking of you and Jamie today. Remember him beating us all at crazy golf?” Chris rings him that evening and talks about Jamie for an hour, laughing and crying.

On the first anniversary, the four of them go to the grave together and then to the pub, where Chris tells stories about Jamie all evening. Mike notices that saying his name out loud does not break anything. It is the opposite.
observe: Notice how people around you behave at a funeral or memorial: who comes, what they do with their bodies, what they say.
Notice whether people mention the dead by name to the bereaved, and how the bereaved respond.
Notice the rituals in your family or community after a death, and which ones people seem to value most.
Notice someone in your life who was bereaved some months ago, and whether anyone is still asking how they are.

drills.name: One True Sentence
steps: Write three short sentences you could say to someone at a funeral, each true and simple.
Write three things you will not say, because they explain or minimise the loss.
Say the three true sentences aloud until they sound like you.
Keep them somewhere you can find them.
variations: Write a true sentence for a colleague's loss and one for a close friend's, and notice how they differ.
Ask someone who has been bereaved which sentences they still remember hearing, both the good ones and the bad.

drills.name: Dates That Matter
steps: List the people you know who have been bereaved in the past few years.
For each, find out or recall the date of the death and the dead person's birthday, if you can.
Put reminders in your phone for those dates.
On the next one, send a short message that uses the dead person's name.
variations: Add the birthdays of the people who died, as well as the dates of their deaths.
Send one message this month to someone whose loss was several years ago, using the dead person's name.

drills.name: The Shiva Visit
steps: Next time you visit someone who is bereaved, go without a prepared speech.
Sit near them, at their level, and wait for them to speak first.
Follow wherever they take the conversation, including into silence or small talk.
Leave when they signal they are tired, and say when you will come back.
Afterwards, write down what you noticed about waiting.
variations: Practise waiting in silence for a minute in an ordinary conversation, to get used to how it feels.
Ask a friend from a different faith or culture how visitors to a house of mourning are expected to behave there.

drills.name: The Months After
steps: Think of someone bereaved three to twelve months ago.
Write one side-by-side invitation you could make: a walk, a match, a job.
Make it this week, and if they say no, ask again in a few weeks.
Note any signs that their grief is turning into something heavier, and decide what you would do if you were worried.
variations: Make the invitation a regular one, such as a monthly walk, rather than a single event.
If the person says no three times, change the invitation to something smaller, such as a short visit with a coffee.

quiz.q: A friend says you should never mention a dead person's name to the bereaved, because it will only upset them. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right; it is kinder to avoid the subject completely from now on
Most bereaved people want the dead remembered and their name spoken
Mention the name only once, at the funeral, and never again afterwards
Only family members should ever mention the name of the person who died
quiz.explain: Research on continuing bonds, and accounts from the bereaved, suggest that many people keep a connection with the dead and are hurt more by silence than by remembering. Saying the name and telling stories brings the person back into shared memory.

quiz.q: What did Norton and Gino find about rituals after a loss?
options: Rituals only helped people who believed strongly that they would work
Rituals made grief worse by reminding people of what they had lost
People who performed rituals reported less grief, even non-believers
Rituals helped only when they were religious and performed in public
quiz.explain: People who performed rituals after a loss reported less grief, even if they did not believe rituals worked. Most rituals were private, and the authors suggested they help by restoring a sense of control.

quiz.q: What is the traditional custom for visitors during shiva, the Jewish week of mourning?
options: Visitors greet the mourner loudly, to lift the mood of the house
Visitors give a short speech about the dead as soon as they arrive
Visitors avoid the mourner and talk only with each other in another room
Visitors sit and wait for the mourner to speak first
quiz.explain: Visitors traditionally wait for the mourner to speak first, a custom traced to Job's friends sitting in silence with him. It lets the mourner decide what they need: to talk about the dead, about something else, or not at all.

quiz.q: Your colleague's father has died. You barely knew the father and do not know what to say. Should you go to the funeral?
options: Yes; go, say one short true sentence, and stand near him
No; you might say the wrong thing and upset him on the day
Only if he asks you directly to come, so you are not intruding
No; send a long message instead explaining why you stayed away
quiz.explain: Bereaved people remember who turned up far more than what anyone said. A short, true sentence and your presence are enough.

quiz.q: What does the wider research on funerals and grief rituals suggest, beyond Norton and Gino's study?
options: Every grief ritual reliably shortens grief for everyone who does it
The evidence is mixed; funerals mattered to later grief, other rituals less
Rituals have been shown to cause prolonged grief in most mourners
Funerals have no connection at all with how grief unfolds over time
quiz.explain: Earlier reviews found little consistent link between rituals and later grief. During the pandemic, funeral attendance and how people felt about the funeral were linked to later grief symptoms, while other rituals were not.

quiz.q: Six months after his wife's death, a friend says he is fine. Most people have stopped calling, and you notice he is drinking more. What fits this chapter best?
options: Take him at his word and give him space, since he has said he is fine
Tell him it is time to move on and get back to normal life
Keep inviting him, mark the dates, and ask directly if you are worried
Wait for him to contact you when he is ready to see people again
quiz.explain: The months after a death are often the hardest, just as support falls away. Keep turning up, mark anniversaries, watch for grief turning into something heavier, and ask directly about suicide if you are worried.

quiz.q: What did Klass, Silverman and Nickman argue about grief?
options: Many bereaved people keep a continuing bond with the person who died
Healthy grief always means letting go of the dead completely within a year
Grief follows five fixed stages that everyone must pass through in order
People who keep memories of the dead are failing to grieve properly
quiz.explain: They challenged the older view that healthy grief means letting go, arguing that many people keep a continuing bond through memories, rituals and conversations. Saying the dead person's name honours it.

quiz.q: A colleague returns to work two weeks after his father's funeral. Everyone is avoiding the subject and he is eating alone. What fits this chapter best?
options: Carry on avoiding the subject, since mentioning it would only upset him
Ask him for the details of how his father died, so that he can talk about it
Say you're sorry, use his dad's name if you can, and offer ordinary company
Tell him that time heals everything and that he will feel better soon
quiz.explain: Silence meant kindly often feels like erasure. A short, true acknowledgement, followed by ordinary warmth such as an invitation to lunch, tells him that his loss has been noticed.

quiz.q: Someone says that men grieve alone and do not need to mourn together. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since men always prefer to keep their grief entirely private
Many men grieve well alongside others, in rituals and shared tasks
It is right for older men, though younger men like to mourn in groups
It is wrong, since men must talk about their feelings in order to grieve
quiz.explain: Many men grieve best side by side: carrying a coffin, telling stories at the usual table, cleaning a headstone together. Shared rituals give grief a form that does not depend on words.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific loss in your life, your own or a friend's. Describe who turned up, what they did with their bodies, and what you remember them saying, if anything. Was there someone who stayed away, or someone who was still there months later? Then think about how you have mourned with others: what you did at funerals, whether you said the dead person's name, whether you kept turning up. What would you do differently next time?
reflection.guidance: Grief can be heavy to write about. Go gently, and stop if you need to. Focus on concrete actions: arriving, sitting, carrying, saying a name, sending a message on an anniversary. If you stayed away from someone's grief because you did not know what to say, you are in very large company; the point is what you do next. If this brings up grief of your own that feels too heavy, the support resources in this app are there.

failureMode: The first failure is to stay away because you do not know what to say, when bereaved people remember presence far more than words. The second is to fill the silence with explanations and platitudes, rather than letting the mourner speak first. The third is to avoid the dead person's name, so that the bereaved feel their loved one has been erased. The fourth is to disappear after the funeral, just as the hardest months begin. And the fifth is to miss grief turning into something heavier, drinking, withdrawal or thoughts of suicide, in a man who keeps saying he is fine. Turn up, stand near, let him speak first, say the name, and keep coming back.

moreCases.title: The colleague who came back
moreCases.scene:
Imran, forty-four, returns to work two weeks after his father's funeral. His team of eight knew, because his manager sent an email. On his
  first morning back, people say good morning and then look at their screens. In the kitchen, two colleagues stop talking when he walks in, say
  hello and leave. Nobody mentions his father. At lunch, he eats at his desk, and the usual invitation to the café does not come.

  By the afternoon, Imran feels invisible. He tells his wife that evening that it was as if nothing had happened, and that he does not know whether
  to be relieved or hurt.

  His colleagues, meanwhile, are talking about him in the pub. Several say they did not know what to say, and did not want to upset him. One says she
  bought a card and left it in her drawer.

Imran's father had been ill for a year, and Imran had taken time off for appointments and hospital visits. Several colleagues had covered for him without being asked. He had been looking forward, in a strange way, to thanking them, and nobody gave him the chance.

Imran also notices that someone has moved the photograph of his father, taken at the office family day two years ago, from his desk. He finds it later in his drawer, face down. Whoever moved it meant well, and he puts it back.

Imran's manager had asked the team, in her email, to be kind to him when he came back. Several of them took that to mean leaving him alone.
moreCases.misread:
Imran's colleagues read silence as tact: the kindest thing, they thought, was to treat him normally and not remind him. Imran read their silence as indifference, as if his father's death had been erased from the office.

The card left in the drawer was the clearest sign of their misreading. The kindness was there; the courage to deliver it was not.

And by not inviting him to lunch, they took away the one ordinary thing that might have helped him feel that his life was carrying on.

The colleague who moved the photograph made the same mistake in a smaller form: trying to protect Imran by removing his father from view.
moreCases.betterRead:
Bereaved people often say afterwards that they cannot remember what anyone said, but they remember exactly who acknowledged the loss and who did not. Silence meant kindly often lands as erasure. The better approach is a short, true acknowledgement, followed by ordinary warmth. The next morning, Imran's colleague Pete brought him a tea, put it on his desk, and said, "I'm really sorry about your dad, mate. I'm around if you want a coffee." Then he went back to his own desk. The colleague with the card gave it to him, and wrote in it that she remembered Imran talking about his father's allotment. Their manager, Sue, asked him privately whether he wanted the team to say anything, and whether he needed flexibility over the next few months. At lunch, Pete invited him to the café, and they talked about football. On the way back, Imran said that his dad would have hated the café's coffee, and laughed for the first time in a fortnight.

Imran also told Sue, later, that the tea had meant more than any card.

moreCases.title: The funeral he did not go to
moreCases.scene:
Dan, thirty-two, gets a message from his best friend, Luke, saying that Luke's mother has died and that the funeral is next Thursday. Dan met
  her twice, briefly. He has an important meeting on Thursday, and he feels awkward about going to the funeral of someone he hardly knew, in a town
  where he will not know anyone. He sends Luke a long, warm message, sends flowers, and does not go.

  At the funeral, Luke looks for him. Afterwards, Luke stops replying to Dan's messages for a few days, and when he does reply, his answers are
  short. When Dan suggests a pint, Luke says he is busy.

  Dan does not understand. He sent flowers and a long message. He did not know Luke's mother. Surely Luke understands.

Luke's mother had been ill for months, and Luke had talked to Dan about it often, on the phone and at the pub. Dan had listened well. He did not realise how much Luke was counting on him to be there at the end.

Dan's sister, when he tells her about Luke's coolness, asks him a single question: if it had been his mother, would he have wanted Luke there? Dan does not answer, because he knows.
moreCases.misread:
Dan read the funeral as an event for the person who died, and so decided that he had little reason to be there. He read his message and flowers as a fair substitute, and Luke's coolness as unreasonable.

He also read his own awkwardness as a reason to stay away, when awkwardness is almost universal at funerals and is rarely a good guide to whether you should go.

Luke, too, did not say what he needed. Many bereaved people do not ask friends to come, and then are hurt when they do not. The safest assumption is that your presence is wanted.
moreCases.betterRead:
Funerals are for the living as much as the dead, and the single most important thing a friend can do when someone is bereaved is to turn up. Luke was not looking for someone who had known his mother; he was looking for his best friend. Messages and flowers are kind, but they cannot stand in a crematorium car park beside someone. Luke's short replies and his refusal of the pint were the signs of a man hurt by an absence, and Dan's better response, once his sister pointed it out, was to repair it in person. He drove to Luke's house the following Saturday, without warning, and said on the doorstep, "I should have been there on Thursday. I'm sorry. I'm here now." Luke looked at him for a long moment, and then let him in. They spent the afternoon sorting through his mother's photographs. Dan learned more about her in four hours than in the two times he had met her, and went to the scattering of her ashes a month later.

Dan also put the date of Luke's mother's death in his calendar, and rang Luke on the first anniversary.

moreCases.title: The pub after the funeral
moreCases.scene:
Tony, fifty-five, died suddenly of a heart attack. After his funeral, his six closest friends go to the pub where they have met on Friday nights
  for thirty years. They sit at their usual table, with Tony's chair empty. For the first hour, they tell stories: the time Tony drove to Wembley with
  the handbrake on, the karaoke, the fishing trip when he fell in. They laugh until they cry. Then they raise their glasses to the empty chair.

  As the evening goes on, one of them, Kev, who was closest to Tony, drinks faster than the others. By ten, he is on his sixth pint, his voice is
  getting louder and angrier, and he says, twice, that it should have been him.

  The others look at each other. Nobody knows what to do. One suggests they let him get it out of his system.

Kev had seen Tony the day before he died, and they had argued about something trivial, a football result. Kev has not told any of the others.

Ian has known Kev for thirty years and has never seen him like this. Kev is the one who organises everything, the one who drove Tony to hospital when he broke his leg, the one who always knows what to say. Tonight he has said almost nothing except about the drink.

Behind the bar, the landlord, who knew Tony for twenty years, has put a pint on the empty chair's side of the table and said it is on the house. Several of the men have stopped and looked at it for a long time.
moreCases.misread:
The group read Kev's heavy drinking and anger as part of the evening's grief, something he needed to get out of his system. That was partly right. It also missed the moment when shared mourning was turning, for one of them, into something more dangerous.

And their reluctance to intervene came partly from respect: nobody wanted to spoil a ritual that meant so much. Looking after someone within the ritual turned out to be possible.

And the suggestion to let him get it out of his system assumed that drink would help him release the grief, when it was more likely to deepen the guilt.
moreCases.betterRead:
Rituals give the body something to do with grief, and the friends' evening was a ritual in all but name: the usual table, the empty chair, the stories, the raised glasses. Norton and Gino found that people who performed rituals after a loss reported less grief, even when they did not believe that rituals worked. But mourning together also means watching each other. Kev's drinking, his rising anger and his repeated "it should have been me" were signs, as Part II described, that his grief might be carrying guilt and that his safety deserved attention. The better response was not to stop the ritual but to look after him within it. His friend Ian moved to sit beside him, got him a glass of water, and later walked him home. On the way, Ian asked him directly whether he was thinking of hurting himself, as 2.13 describes. Kev said no, just that he missed him. Ian rang him the next day, and the next, and they went fishing in Tony's honour a month later.

Kev told Ian, months later, about the argument the day before Tony died. Ian said Tony would have laughed about it.

moreCases.title: The headstone on his birthday
moreCases.scene:
Martin, sixty, lost his son, Josh, to cancer three years ago, at twenty-four. On Josh's birthday each year, Martin goes to the cemetery alone,
  early in the morning, and sits by the grave. He has never told anyone that he does this. His wife goes later in the day, with flowers.

  This year, three of Josh's friends from school, now in their late twenties, message Martin to ask whether they could come with him. They say they
  think about Josh on his birthday and would like to do something. Martin is touched and unsure. He has always done this alone.

  He says yes. They meet at the cemetery gates at eight. Nobody quite knows what to say.

Josh's friends have also kept a group chat going since he died, in which they share photos and memories of him, especially on his birthday and the anniversary. Martin did not know it existed until one of them mentioned it at the gates.

Martin has never been good at talking about Josh. In the first year, friends asked how he was and he said fine, and then they stopped asking. His wife talks about Josh often; Martin finds that he cannot, except at the grave, alone, where he talks to Josh out loud.

At the gates, the three friends stand in a loose group, hands in pockets, looking at the ground. One of them, Sam, is holding a carrier bag. Martin shakes their hands and says it is good of them to come, and then there is a silence that none of them knows how to fill.
moreCases.misread:
Martin read his private visits as the way a father should grieve, quietly and alone. Josh's friends were not sure whether they would be intruding on something that belonged to the family.

Martin also read his solitude as a choice, when it may have been partly that nobody had ever offered to come with him.

And the friends' hesitation, whether they would be intruding, came from respect. Many people hold back from shared mourning because they think grief belongs only to the family, when the family often longs for others to share it.

Josh's friends, too, had been unsure for three years whether they were allowed to grieve him, since he was not their son. Asking Martin was the first time any of them had said aloud that they missed him.
moreCases.betterRead:
Klass, Silverman and Nickman argued that many bereaved people keep a continuing bond with the person who has died, through memories, rituals, conversations and places, and that this is not a failure to move on but part of grieving well. Shared rituals can carry that bond for several people at once. The better approach was to give the morning something to do, side by side. One of the friends, Sam, had brought a bucket, brushes and a cloth. Together, the four of them cleaned the headstone, pulled the weeds round it and put fresh flowers in the holder, mostly in silence. Then they sat on the grass and told stories about Josh that Martin had never heard. When they left, Martin shook each of their hands and held on. The next year, there were six of them. Martin said that he had thought the birthday would always be the loneliest day of his year, and that it had become one of the best.

Martin also joined the group chat, and started posting photographs of Josh as a boy.

workedReading.title: Visiting a house of mourning
workedReading.scene:
Ravi, forty-two, hears that the wife of his friend Paul has died after a long illness. The funeral is next week. Paul's sister has said that friends are welcome at the house in the evenings. Ravi has never visited a house of mourning before, and he does not know what to say or how long to stay. He decides to go on the second evening.

Ravi knew Helen a little: she used to make the best curry at their summer barbecues, and she once told him off for not wearing sunscreen. He has no idea what he will say to Paul, and he nearly does not go.

He also knows that Paul is not a talker. They play squash together on Tuesdays and talk about work and football. In fifteen years, they have never discussed anything personal, and Ravi has no idea what Paul will want from him.

He also reminds himself that he does not have to get it right. Paul will be surrounded by people for days, and nobody expects any of them to say the perfect thing.

steps.label: Arrive and greet
steps.text:
At the door, Paul's sister lets him in. Paul is in the living room with several relatives. Ravi walks over and matches what Paul offers. Paul stands and holds out his hand; Ravi takes it, holds it a moment longer than usual, and puts his other hand on Paul's arm. Paul's face crumples slightly, and he pulls Ravi into a brief hug. Ravi leans into it and lets Paul end it.

He also leaves his coat on the hook in the hall rather than keeping it on. A coat kept on says a visitor is about to leave, and he wants to stay for a while.

He also notices that Paul's hand is cold and slightly shaky, and that his face is grey with tiredness. Paul has been greeting people for two days, and every greeting costs him something.

steps.label: One true sentence
steps.text:
Ravi says, "I'm so sorry about Helen." He does not add that she is in a better place, that it was a blessing after so long, or that he knows how Paul feels. One true sentence, using her name, is enough. He has rehearsed it in the car so that it would come out steadily.

He also resists the urge to add anything about Helen's illness, or how hard it must have been to watch. Those sentences would ask Paul to relive it, in front of relatives.

He also says it quietly, close enough for Paul to hear but not for the whole room, so that the moment belongs to the two of them.

steps.label: Sit, and wait
steps.text:
Paul sits down again, and Ravi sits near him, at his level, rather than standing among the relatives. He does not launch into conversation. He waits, as visitors do during shiva, for Paul to speak first, so that Paul can decide whether to talk about Helen, about something else, or not at all.

He also leaves his phone in his coat. In a house of mourning, a phone in the hand says that a visitor's attention is somewhere else.

He also notices the other relatives' patterns: some talking loudly, some sitting very still, one crying in a corner. Mourning looks different in every body in the room, and none of it needs correcting.

He also chooses a seat beside Paul rather than opposite, so that Paul can look at him or away as he likes. In grief, as in so much else, side by side asks less.

steps.label: Follow his lead
steps.text:
After a minute, Paul says that Helen would have hated all these people in the house. Ravi smiles and says she always liked a quiet night in. Paul laughs, and starts telling a story about their honeymoon. Ravi listens, asks a question, and lets Paul talk. When Paul falls silent and looks at the floor, Ravi stays silent too.

He also shares a memory of his own when it fits: the time Helen told him off about the sunscreen. Paul laughs again and says that was exactly like her. Small, specific memories are among the gifts visitors can bring.

He also notices that Paul's voice changes when he talks about the honeymoon, lighter and quicker, as if remembering her alive gives him a moment's rest from remembering her dying.

steps.label: Make yourself useful
steps.text:
When the doorbell rings for the third time, Ravi says, "I'll get it," and answers the door for the next visitors. He makes a round of tea for the relatives. Practical help gives his body something to do, and it takes small burdens off a family who have been on their feet for days.

He also asks Paul's sister, quietly, whether there is anything else the family needs: lifts to the funeral, someone to collect relatives from the station, someone to walk the dog.

He also washes up the tea cups before he leaves. Small, practical acts in a house of mourning are noticed and remembered, often more than anything said.

He also leaves the kitchen tidier than he found it, without making a fuss of it.

steps.label: Leave when he tires
steps.text:
After about an hour, Ravi notices that Paul's answers are getting shorter and that he keeps rubbing his eyes. He stands, says he will let him rest, and puts his hand on Paul's shoulder. He says, "I'll be at the funeral on Tuesday, and I'll ring you next weekend."

He also says goodbye to the relatives he met, not only to Paul. A visit to a house of mourning is a visit to the family, and everyone there is grieving.

He also tells Paul's sister that he will be at the funeral, so that she knows to expect him, and asks whether they need anyone to help carry the coffin or give a reading.

steps.label: Keep the promise
steps.text:
Ravi goes to the funeral and rings the following weekend. He puts the date of Helen's death in his phone. Three months later, he invites Paul to a match. Paul says no, and Ravi asks again a few weeks later, and this time Paul says yes. On the anniversary, Ravi sends a message that says only, "Thinking of you and Helen today." Paul replies that he had not expected anyone to remember.

He also notes that he had nearly not gone because he did not know what to say, and that he had said almost nothing, and that it had been enough.

Paul tells him, a year later, that he does not remember anything anyone said in the first week, but that he remembers Ravi answering the door.

moreFailures.title: Staying away because you do not know what to say
moreFailures.body:
The commonest reason men give for not visiting the bereaved, not going to funerals and not calling is that they do not know what to say. Bereaved people almost never remember what was said. They remember who was there. A man who turns up, says one short true sentence and then sits with them has done more than one who sends a long, eloquent message and stays away. If you are not sure whether to go, go. If you are not sure what to say, say that you are sorry, use the dead person's name, and then let the mourner lead.

It also helps to remember that turning up can take many forms: going to the funeral, visiting the house, delivering food, standing at the back of a crematorium, sitting in the pub afterwards. Any of these counts.

It also helps to remember that it is never too late to turn up. A visit a week after the funeral, or a month, is still welcome, and often more so, because by then most people have stopped coming.

It also helps to take your cue from the family about the kind of presence they want. Some families want a crowd; others want a few close friends. A short message asking "Would a visit help, or would you rather have some quiet?" lets them choose.

moreFailures.title: Filling the silence with platitudes
moreFailures.body:
At a funeral or in a house of mourning, silence feels unbearable to many visitors, and they fill it: "She's in a better place", "At least he's not suffering", "Everything happens for a reason", "I know how you feel". Each of these explains or minimises the loss, and many bereaved people find them hurtful. The custom of waiting for the mourner to speak first, as visitors do during shiva, is wiser: you cannot know what the mourner needs, so let them decide. Sit near them, at their level, and be comfortable with silence. It is part of the comfort.

It also helps to resist telling your own story of loss. However well meant, it turns the conversation towards you, and the mourner may feel obliged to comfort you.

It also helps to watch your own discomfort. Platitudes usually come from the visitor's need to fill a silence, not from the mourner's need to hear them. Noticing that need, and letting it pass, is most of the skill.

It also helps to remember that the mourner may want to talk about the dead person, not about their own feelings. "Tell me about her" is often easier to answer than "How are you feeling?"

moreFailures.title: Avoiding the dead person's name
moreFailures.body:
Many people avoid saying a dead person's name to the bereaved, afraid of opening a wound. Most bereaved people say that what hurts more is the silence: the sense that the person they loved has been erased from everyone else's conversation. Klass and colleagues described how many people keep a continuing bond with the dead, and saying the name is one of the simplest ways to honour it. "I was thinking about Jamie today" or "Helen would have loved this" are often received with tears, and with gratitude.

It also helps to know that saying the name may bring tears, and that tears are not a sign you have done harm. They are often a sign that you have made it safe to grieve.

It also helps to keep using the name over the years. A father who lost a son ten years ago may still long to hear someone else say it, and almost nobody does.

And when you do say the name, say it naturally, in an ordinary sentence. A name said in a hushed, careful voice can feel like a performance; said warmly and lightly, it feels like the person is still part of things.

moreFailures.title: Disappearing after the funeral
moreFailures.body:
In the first week after a death, there are visitors, flowers and food. By the third month, most of it has gone, just as the numbness wears off and the full weight of the loss arrives. The men who matter most are the ones who keep turning up: who invite the bereaved man to the things they used to do together, keep asking when he says no, remember the dates and say the name. Put the date of the death and the dead person's birthday in your phone. On those days, send a short message. It is one of the most remembered kindnesses there is.

It also helps to remember the men who are often overlooked: fathers who have lost a baby, men whose partners have died young, men grieving a friend rather than a relative. Their grief is often less recognised, and the months after can be especially lonely.

It also helps to keep the invitations ordinary. A bereaved man may not want to talk about his loss every time you meet; he may want, more than anything, a normal evening, with his loss acknowledged and then left alone.

It also helps to tell the bereaved man that you will keep checking in, so that the calls do not feel like intrusions. "I'm going to ring you every couple of weeks, if that's all right" makes it easy for him to accept.

questions.q: What should I say at a funeral?
questions.a:
Very little, and something true. "I'm so sorry about your dad." "I'm so sorry. He was a great man." "I'm thinking of you." Use the dead person's name if you can. Avoid explaining the death, minimising it or comparing it to your own losses. If you have a short, specific memory, it can be a gift: "I'll always remember him teaching us to fish." Then let the mourner lead. If you cannot speak because you are too moved, a hand on the arm or a held handshake says the same thing. Nobody at a funeral needs eloquence. They need people who came.

It also helps to say goodbye properly when you leave a funeral or a wake. A hand on the shoulder and "I'll ring you next week" turns your presence into a promise.

It also helps to know that you do not have to say anything at all. A firm handshake, a hand on the arm or a hug, held for a moment, can say everything that needs saying.

It also helps to say something to the other mourners, not only the closest relative. Parents, siblings and friends of the dead often stand at the edge of a funeral, unnoticed.

questions.q: Should I go to a funeral if I barely knew the person who died?
questions.a:
Usually, yes, if you know someone who is grieving. Funerals are for the living as much as for the dead, and many bereaved people say that seeing friends, colleagues and neighbours there, people who came for their sake, was one of the things that helped most. Dan's case in this chapter shows how much an absence can hurt. If you cannot go, say so honestly, send a message, and find a way to turn up afterwards: a visit, a meal, a walk. If you are unsure whether you would be welcome, ask a family member or simply go and stand at the back.

It also helps to know that at many funerals, especially large ones, the family will not remember everyone who came, but they will read the book of condolence or the cards later, and notice who was there.

It also helps to think about who else might be there: the dead person's colleagues, neighbours and friends. A funeral full of people who came for the family's sake tells them that their loved one mattered to more people than they knew.

questions.q: How long should I keep checking in?
questions.a:
Longer than most people do. The hardest months for many bereaved people are the third to the twelfth, after the visitors have gone, and the first anniversary, the first birthday and the first Christmas are often very hard. Grief can stay intense for a long time after the loss of a child or a partner. Keep inviting, keep asking, keep saying the name, for at least the first year and on the anniversaries after that. A message on the anniversary five years later can mean as much as one in the first week, because by then almost nobody else remembers.

It also helps to remember the other people who are grieving: the dead person's parents, siblings, children and friends. A message to them on the anniversary can mean as much as one to the closest relative.

It also helps to keep the messages short and to ask for nothing. "Thinking of you and Helen today" needs no reply, and the person receiving it does not have to manage your feelings as well as their own.

It also helps to notice when he starts mentioning the person who died on his own. That is often a sign that he wants to talk about them, and a good moment to ask a question or share a memory.

questions.q: Is it all right to laugh at a wake?
questions.a:
Yes. Many wakes are full of laughter, as people tell stories about the person who died, and the laughter is often part of the grief, not a break from it. The chapter on grief in Part II described a widow laughing at her husband's wake and sobbing in the toilets an hour later; both were grief. Follow the mood of the family. If they are telling funny stories, join in. If they are quiet, be quiet. What matters is that the laughter is about the person and shared with the mourners, not at anyone's expense.

It also helps to tell your own story about the person, if you have one. A funny or warm story at a wake is often the most welcome thing a guest can offer.

It also helps to watch for the people who are not laughing. A wake can be hard for someone whose grief is raw, and sitting quietly with them for a while is as important as joining the stories.

It also helps to know that some cultures and faiths have very different customs for mourning, including restrictions on music, laughter or food. If you are attending a funeral in a tradition you do not know, ask someone what is expected.

questions.q: What if my friend grieves by working?
questions.a:
Then join him. Many men lean towards what Doka and Martin called instrumental grief: they grieve by doing, organising the funeral, building something, fixing the house, clearing the dead person's things. That is a way of grieving, not a failure to grieve. Offer to help with the task: carrying, driving, sorting, mending. Side by side, with something to do, many men talk more about the person who died than they ever would face to face. And watch, gently, for signs that the work has become a way of never stopping, which can wear a man down, and use the pauses to ask how he is.

It also helps to make the task his choice. Offering to help with something he wants to do is different from taking it over, and he may need to do some of it himself as part of grieving.

It also helps to remember the practical tasks that follow a death, such as clearing a house, dealing with paperwork, selling a car. These can be overwhelming, and help with them is often the most welcome kind.

It also helps to remember that sorting a dead person's belongings can be one of the hardest tasks of all. Offering to help, and then following his lead about what to keep, is a kindness he may never forget.

questions.q: What about losses when people could not gather?
questions.a:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, many people lost someone without being able to visit them, hold a full funeral or gather afterwards, and research such as Mitima-Verloop and colleagues' 2022 study found that restricted mourning was linked to harder grief for many. Something similar happens when people die far away or when families cannot travel. It can help to create a ritual later: a memorial gathering on an anniversary, a walk to a place the person loved, a meal in their honour. It is never too late to mourn together, and many families find that a later gathering helps.

It also helps to involve people who could not be there at the time. A memorial gathering a year later, with photographs and stories, can give them the chance to mourn that they missed.

It also helps to involve the person who could not be there in planning it. A son who could not attend his father's funeral may want to choose the readings or the music for a later memorial.

And if you are the one who could not be there, it is worth telling the family that you are grieving too, and asking whether there is anything you can do now. Absence at the time does not have to mean absence for good.

watch.title: Manchester by the Sea: Official Trailer
watch.notice: A man returns home after his brother's death. Watch how the men around him handle grief together: brief embraces, practical tasks, few words, and long silences that are a kind of company.

reviewPrompt: This week, put the dates of one friend's loss in your phone, and next time someone is bereaved, turn up and let them speak first.
